title: From Up or Out to Up and Out
author: Anthea Roberts · David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s infrastructure thesis and materially extends it by framing Harvey as a shared platform for multidisciplinary delivery, while identifying deployment businesses, AI-native providers, the Big Four and in-house orchestration as competing service models. It also develops the cluster’s staffing implications through the proposed shift from production to orchestration, while keeping competitive durability and institutional protection unresolved.
qs: The legalization of AI creates a new and expanding domain of "out."  Harvey Shared Spaces is an example of building infrastructure for this --- law firms, consulting firms, and corporate clients in the same AI-powered workspace on the same matter, doing digitally what Eversheds tried to do physically and Bridgewater tried to orchestrate manually.

They sell neither tools nor billable hours but deployment: the integrated, cross-domain delivery that "up and out" describes, built from the start on an AI cost structure and carrying none of the partnership overhead.

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source accepts integrated, multidisciplinary delivery as the central competitive terrain and acknowledges that the Big Four have not yet displaced leading law firms. It materially extends the synthesis by arguing that moving upmarket is not durable protection and that AI-enabled deployment businesses could intensify integrated-service competition, while treating future disruption as a prediction rather than an established outcome.
qs: The Big Four have been building integrated solutions capability for decades --- consulting, audit, tax, technology, and global infrastructure at a scale no law firm can match.
To be sure, the Big 4 have yet to fully capitalize on this advantage.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source accepts that AI can strengthen corporate legal departments and redesign delivery, then materially extends the proposition through its concept of the general counsel as an orchestrator of autonomous systems, professional expertise and integrated solutions. It also qualifies buyer capture as a competitive possibility rather than an assured outcome, given rival providers and incumbent law firms’ structural defenses.
qs: But "up and out" suggests a third: the orchestrator.
Meanwhile, general counsel aren't waiting --- they're building their own orchestration capability, assembling integrated solutions without law firms as the intermediary.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s account of increasingly overlapping provider roles and materially extends it with reported 2026 foundation-model deployment businesses. It also sharpens the competitive taxonomy by distinguishing integrated, cross-domain deployment from both software sales and traditional billable-hour services, while presenting the Big Four’s AI advantage as a conditional prediction rather than an established outcome.
qs: They sell neither tools nor billable hours but deployment: the integrated, cross-domain delivery that "up and out" describes, built from the start on an AI cost structure and carrying none of the partnership overhead.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s end-to-end, multidisciplinary delivery proposition and materially extends it with “up and out”: lawyers acting as orchestrators who commission autonomous systems, use assistive systems and supply integrative judgment. It also identifies shared AI workspaces as enabling infrastructure while acknowledging unresolved competitive and regulatory constraints.
qs: The legalization of AI creates a new and expanding domain of "out."  Harvey Shared Spaces is an example of building infrastructure for this --- law firms, consulting firms, and corporate clients in the same AI-powered workspace on the same matter, doing digitally what Eversheds tried to do physically and Bridgewater tried to orchestrate manually.
Someone who commissions autopilots, works with copilots, and exercises the integrative judgment that neither can replicate.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts that AI compresses junior volume work, threatening both pyramid economics and the expertise pipeline. It materially extends the cluster by proposing “up and out” orchestration and a diamond-shaped staffing model, while identifying a profession-wide training free-rider problem that could erode future verification capacity.
qs: "Up *or* out" is becoming "up *and* out." As automation compresses the base of the pyramid, the lawyers who remain are being pushed simultaneously *up* the value chain, toward higher-order judgment, and *out* into adjacent domains that were never strictly legal.
And it gets worse: the verification capacity needed to catch increasingly subtle AI errors is exactly the domain expertise that the collective automation decision is destroying.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts that AI is a business-model and market-structure problem rather than merely a productivity tool. It materially extends the synthesis through its “up and out” strategy: automation narrows junior-heavy staffing while lawyers shift toward higher-order judgment and orchestration across multidisciplinary, client-controlled ecosystems. It also preserves the cluster’s uncertainty about whether professional and regulatory protections will prevent disruption or only slow it.
qs: "Up *or* out" is becoming "up *and* out." As automation compresses the base of the pyramid, the lawyers who remain are being pushed simultaneously *up* the value chain, toward higher-order judgment, and *out* into adjacent domains that were never strictly legal.
Meanwhile, general counsel aren't waiting --- they're building their own orchestration capability, assembling integrated solutions without law firms as the intermediary.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account that AI automates bounded junior work while shifting lawyers toward judgment rather than wholesale replacement. It materially extends that account through the “up and out” model: elite lawyers become cross-domain orchestrators of autonomous and assistive systems. It also reinforces the cluster’s apprenticeship concern by identifying domain expertise as a scarce capability endangered when the pyramid’s training work is automated, while acknowledging that moving upmarket may be defensive retreat rather than successful adaptation.
qs: "Up *or* out" is becoming "up *and* out." As automation compresses the base of the pyramid, the lawyers who remain are being pushed simultaneously *up* the value chain, toward higher-order judgment, and *out* into adjacent domains that were never strictly legal.

In our [previous piece](https://clp.law.harvard.edu/ai-and-the-legal-profession/essays/the-training-crisis.html), we identified domain expertise as the scarcest ingredient in the AI formula --- the one the profession is at risk of losing.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI restructures legal delivery, compresses routine work and shifts bargaining toward in-house teams, AI-native providers and multidisciplinary competitors. It materially extends the synthesis with the “up and out” model: lawyers become orchestrators of AI and cross-domain advice, while four converging provider types contest incumbent firms’ position. Its disagreement over regulatory moats qualifies the likely extent of displacement rather than rejecting the transformation.
qs: "Up *or* out" is becoming "up *and* out." As automation compresses the base of the pyramid, the lawyers who remain are being pushed simultaneously *up* the value chain, toward higher-order judgment, and *out* into adjacent domains that were never strictly legal.
Meanwhile, general counsel aren't waiting --- they're building their own orchestration capability, assembling integrated solutions without law firms as the intermediary.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI-driven value depends on changes in legal production and provider relationships, then materially extends the cluster with a four-direction competitive-convergence account involving AI-native providers, the Big Four, in-house orchestration and foundation-model deployment firms. It also adds regulatory gatekeeping, institutional authority and high-stakes trust as structural limits on disintermediation, while acknowledging that the competitive outcomes remain unresolved and largely unquantified.
qs: Meanwhile, general counsel aren't waiting --- they're building their own orchestration capability, assembling integrated solutions without law firms as the intermediary.
Bar rules, opinion letter requirements, court access restrictions, and licensing regimes create structural moats that technology alone can't breach.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI is more likely to reorganise legal-service production than eliminate lawyers, preserving integrative judgment, trust and institutional authority. It materially extends the cluster by proposing an “up and out” orchestration model and identifying converging competition from AI-native providers, the Big Four, in-house legal departments and foundation-model deployment firms.
qs: So "up and out" faces convergence from four directions simultaneously.

st.t: Staffing structure: AI threatens both pyramid and pipeline
st.an: The source accepts that AI threatens both traditional staffing structures and the development pipeline, then materially extends the proposition by comparing alternative firm shapes, advocating a collaborative diamond, and identifying a collective-action problem in training that could erode the domain expertise required for verification.
qs: This is the shape that looks most promising --- a wide band of orchestrators, reviewers, and integrators working alongside AI, with training reimagined through orchestration rather than volume work.
And it gets worse: the verification capacity needed to catch increasingly subtle AI errors is exactly the domain expertise that the collective automation decision is destroying.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI-created value depends on integrated, multidisciplinary delivery rather than task efficiency alone. It materially extends that proposition by defining lawyers’ emerging role as orchestration and mapping concrete competitors—AI-native firms, the Big Four, client legal departments and capital-backed deployment businesses—seeking to capture that value, while leaving regulatory protection unresolved.
qs: But "up and out" suggests a third: the orchestrator.

They sell neither tools nor billable hours but deployment: the integrated, cross-domain delivery that "up and out" describes, built from the start on an AI cost structure and carrying none of the partnership overhead.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s principal impact is organisational and workflow redesign rather than simple lawyer replacement, and materially extends the cluster by specifying multidisciplinary integrated delivery as the target operating model. It identifies AI-enabled scaling, digital collaboration and AI-native deployment businesses as mechanisms that may reshape provider boundaries and permit competitors to move from routine work toward higher-value services. Its more disruptive claims are predictive and qualified by the Big Four’s continued marginality in established Big Law markets.
qs: Lawyers increasingly work collaboratively with consultants, technologists, strategists, and policy experts on problems that carry legal consequences but require integrated, multi-disciplinary solutions.

They sell neither tools nor billable hours but deployment: the integrated, cross-domain delivery that "up and out" describes, built from the start on an AI cost structure and carrying none of the partnership overhead.

st.t: Workflow control: Foundation models challenge specialist interfaces
st.an: The source accepts that foundation-model companies are moving beyond supplying software and materially extends the proposition by identifying dedicated deployment businesses that compete in integrated, cross-domain legal delivery. It broadens the competitive focus from control of lawyers’ software interface to control of implementation and service delivery, while acknowledging that law’s regulatory and institutional protections may limit displacement.
qs: They sell neither tools nor billable hours but deployment: the integrated, cross-domain delivery that "up and out" describes, built from the start on an AI cost structure and carrying none of the partnership overhead.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that corporate buyers are disaggregating and orchestrating legal delivery, while routine work becomes more exposed to AI-enabled alternatives and consequential advice retains trust-based protections. It materially extends the synthesis by identifying integrated, multidisciplinary delivery—and competition from the Big Four, AI-native firms and foundation-model deployment businesses—as the next stage of workflow reconfiguration, though it does not substantively address junior training or verification.
qs: Meanwhile, general counsel aren't waiting --- they're building their own orchestration capability, assembling integrated solutions without law firms as the intermediary.

kp.k: Automation pushes lawyers toward judgment and adjacent domains
kp.d: The authors argue that automating the pyramid's high-volume base threatens the revenue structure supporting partners and reorients remaining lawyers simultaneously toward higher-order judgment ('up') and multidisciplinary work ('out'). They present this as a possible strategic evolution, not an assured successful response to disruption. Drawing on Julien Bek, they distinguish rule-based intelligence work, such as contract review, due diligence and first-pass research, from experience-based judgment.
qs: The pyramid works because the base subsidises the top

As automation compresses the base of the pyramid, the lawyers who remain are being pushed simultaneously *up* the value chain, toward higher-order judgment, and *out* into adjacent domains that were never strictly legal.
This sounds like strategic evolution. It might be. Or it might be what every disrupted profession tells itself as the ground shifts beneath it.

kp.k: Integrated solutions demand predates generative AI
kp.d: The authors describe Wilkins's framework of movement from autonomous law toward integrated solutions, accelerated by the pandemic, geopolitical conflict, sustainability and social justice issues. They cite Eversheds's consulting arm, PwC promoting legal in 124 countries by 2012, and Bridgewater's Tracey Yurko assembling virtual law firms that cut costs by more than 50 percent. These are reported historical examples, not new empirical findings in this essay.
qs: The demand for integrated solutions predates AI, and multiple actors tried to build it.

Lawyers increasingly work collaboratively with consultants, technologists, strategists, and policy experts on problems that carry legal consequences but require integrated, multi-disciplinary solutions.
PwC promoting legal in 124 countries by 2012
in-house counsel like Bridgewater's Tracey Yurko building "virtual law firms" that cut costs by more than 50 percent

kp.k: AI may ease barriers to multidisciplinary delivery
kp.d: The essay identifies law-firm cultural resistance, ABA Rule 5.4's nonlawyer ownership restrictions, physical integration difficulties and inability to take outside investment as obstacles to earlier integrated-services efforts. The authors argue that shared digital workspaces, agents performing volume work and a common technological platform remove or soften some operational barriers; they do not claim AI itself repeals ownership rules.
qs: AI doesn't create the demand for integrated solutions. It removes some of the barriers that blocked it.
The co-location problem disappears when everyone is in the same digital workspace.
The scaling problem changes when AI agents handle the volume work.
The cultural integration problem softens when the technology itself is the common platform.

kp.k: Orchestration becomes a proposed core lawyer role
kp.d: The authors predict that automating research, drafting and precedent analysis could shift lawyers from producing work to directing, coaching and editing AI outputs using domain expertise and judgment. They explicitly condition the legal prediction on a pattern they identify in software engineering. Their proposed orchestrator commissions autonomous systems, works with assistive systems and integrates recommendations, extending beyond a simple augmentation-versus-replacement binary.
qs: That shift from production to orchestration IS "up." If the pattern holds, law is next.
It requires all lawyers to become managers who are able to direct, coach, and edit output by AI using their domain expertise, taste, and judgment.
But "up and out" suggests a third: the orchestrator.
Someone who commissions autopilots, works with copilots, and exercises the integrative judgment that neither can replicate.

kp.k: Adjacent advisory work includes governing organizational AI
kp.d: The proposed expansion encompasses commercial and tax deal structuring, board governance, reputation, stakeholder management and geopolitical sanctions analysis. The authors also forecast that in-house teams will increasingly govern autonomous-agent deployment through liability frameworks, regulatory expectations and organizational risk tolerance, creating a new domain of legal work.
qs: Governance advisory spanning board dynamics, reputational risk, and stakeholder management.
Sanctions compliance requiring not just the legal rules but the geopolitical logic behind them.
as autonomous AI agents proliferate, in-house teams will increasingly govern how organizations use them --- liability frameworks, regulatory expectations, risk tolerance.

kp.k: Harvey is interpreted as integrated-solutions infrastructure
kp.d: The authors present Harvey Shared Spaces as infrastructure joining law firms, consulting firms and corporate clients on the same matter. Their claim that Harvey seeks integrated-solutions AI with law as its entry point is expressly an interpretation of strategy, not an attributed company statement or demonstrated market outcome.
qs: Harvey Shared Spaces is an example of building infrastructure for this --- law firms, consulting firms, and corporate clients in the same AI-powered workspace on the same matter
In our reading, Harvey isn't aiming to create "legal AI" per se. It's aiming to create integrated solutions AI --- with law as the entry point.

kp.k: Moving upmarket may reproduce Christensen's disruption pattern
kp.d: Using Christensen's theory and historical analogies involving steel minimills and Kodak, the authors warn that ceding low-end work can allow challengers to improve and enter incumbents' premium markets. They apply this as a risk framework for law, not proof of an inevitable outcome. Bek's quoted claim describes outsourced work as an entry point to the larger insourced market.
qs: The disruptors improve. They move upmarket. The low-end work was the wedge; the high-end work was always the target.
"Up and out" is the legal profession's version of moving upmarket.
Steel minimills started with rebar and ended up making sheet steel. Kodak moved to professional film as consumer photography went digital.

kp.k: Big Four capabilities challenge law firms' upmarket strategy
kp.d: The authors report that Wilkins's 2018 Center on the Legal Profession research found many Global 100 firms marketing integrated solutions. They argue that law firms are entering territory already served by the Big Four's consulting, audit, tax, technology and global infrastructure. They qualify the threat: internal ambivalence, legal's small balance-sheet importance and the post-covid surge in high-end legal demand have kept the Big Four marginal in established Big Law markets. AI revitalizing this competition is a possibility, not an established result.
qs: In 2018, David's research at the Center on the Legal Profession found that many Global 100 firms were aggressively marketing themselves as providing integrated solutions
We have lost good partners to Big Four. They will move up the value chain --- no question --- and eat our lunch.
To be sure, the Big 4 have yet to fully capitalize on this advantage.

kp.k: Foundation-model deployment businesses add a new competitive threat
kp.d: The essay reports April–May 2026 developments: Anthropic's $1.5 billion venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and Goldman Sachs, and OpenAI's $4 billion deployment company backed by TPG, with McKinsey, Bain & Company and Capgemini taking equity and Tomoro supplying staff through acquisition. The authors characterize these businesses as forward-deployed engineering operations selling integrated delivery rather than software tools or billable hours, with AI-native costs and no partnership overhead. These are source-reported developments and strategic interpretations.
qs: Anthropic's \$1.5 billion joint venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs; OpenAI's \$4 billion deployment company, backed by TPG with McKinsey, Bain & Company, and Capgemini taking equity, staffed from day one by its acquisition of the applied-AI consultancy Tomoro.
All run Palantir's model --- forward-deployed engineers who live inside the client's complexity rather than shipping software and leaving.
They sell neither tools nor billable hours but deployment

kp.d: The authors identify technical-work displacement by AI-native providers, lateral entry by the Big Four, buyers building their own orchestration, and foundation-model deployment businesses as simultaneous pressures. They additionally describe capital entering delivery through a cap-table software company's acquisition of a regulated law firm and announced ambitions beyond routine work. General counsel's ability to assemble services without law firms as intermediaries threatens firms' proposed orchestration position.
qs: Meanwhile, general counsel aren't waiting --- they're building their own orchestration capability, assembling integrated solutions without law firms as the intermediary.
From below: AI-native firms eating technical work, accumulating data, improving.
Laterally: Big Four adding legal to their existing integrated infrastructure.
From the client side: general counsel building their own orchestration layer.
And from the AI substrate itself: foundation-model deployment firms selling integrated solutions at a cost structure no partnership can match.

kp.k: Wilkins emphasizes regulatory defenses and professional control
kp.d: Wilkins's position is that licensing, court-access restrictions, opinion-letter requirements, institutional trust and law's regulatory embedding constitute real defenses. He also argues that lawyers' control over regulation, partnerships and professional culture slows market restructuring relative to software. This concerns the pace and potential durability of legal institutions, rather than a demonstrated guarantee against substitution.
qs: David has documented law's structural defenses for decades and believes they're real.
Bar rules, opinion letter requirements, court access restrictions, and licensing regimes create structural moats that technology alone can't breach.
A software market reconfigures at the speed the technology allows; a legal market reconfigures at the speed its people permit.
The convergence we have described is arriving more slowly into law than it has into less protected industries, and it will keep arriving more slowly.

kp.k: Automation could complement rather than replace senior judgment
kp.d: The essay advances a conditional counterargument to Christensen: increased automated contract and compliance volumes may generate more edge cases, cross-jurisdictional trade-offs and strategic risk decisions requiring human judgment. If these effects increase apex demand, automation and senior legal work could be complements. The authors distinguish this proposed mechanism from digital photography's displacement of professional film and include AI governance as a new work category.
qs: when AI increases the volume of automated contracts, it also increases edge cases requiring human judgment.
If automation *feeds* the apex --- creating demand for the integrative judgment "up and out" produces --- then the relationship between base and apex isn't substitution. It's complementarity.
But automated legal intelligence might well create more demand for legal judgment.

kp.k: Roberts argues regulatory friction is not immunity
kp.d: Roberts counters that protections in other professions did not prevent disruption from routing around them. She argues that lawyer-supervised AI-native platforms can preserve regulatory compliance while changing economics, and that the boundary between judgment and automatable intelligence keeps moving. The essay cites Arizona licensing KPMG, Utah's sandbox and the May 2026 developments as pressure on existing barriers. The authors explicitly leave their disagreement unresolved.
qs: Friction is not the same as immunity.
AI-native legal platforms don't breach the bar; they maintain lawyer oversight while delivering AI-native economics.
Tasks that were considered pure architectural judgment eighteen months ago in software engineering are now handled by AI agents.
Arizona granted KPMG a law license, Utah created a regulatory sandbox
The honest answer: we don't know.

kp.k: Obelisk and barbell scenarios imply different staffing losses
kp.d: The authors propose, rather than observe as settled outcomes, an obelisk retaining hierarchy and up-or-out promotion with dramatically reduced junior intake, and a barbell combining senior relationship-holders with AI-native juniors while squeezing mid-career lawyers. In the barbell scenario, loss of progressively complex middle-career experience breaks the pipeline into senior integrative judgment.
qs: It's the pyramid's answer to automation: keep the structure, shrink the intake.
Senior partners at the top --- the judgment layer, the client relationships, the institutional weight.
AI-native juniors at the bottom --- fluent in the tools, cheap to deploy with AI leverage, productive from day one in ways previous generations weren't.
But over time, this becomes a structural problem because the pipeline of producing people that move from the bottom to the top is broken.

kp.k: Diamond staffing risks collective underinvestment in training
kp.d: The proposed diamond concentrates staff in human–AI collaboration, with orchestrators, reviewers and integrators between a thin junior base and a thin senior apex. Although the authors consider this promising, they argue that individually rational automation and hiring trained lawyers create a collective training free-rider problem. This could destroy precisely the domain expertise needed for human verification of subtle AI errors.
qs: Thick in the middle where human-AI collaboration is densest, thin at the automated base and the pure-judgment apex.
No firm needs to train lawyers; it needs *trained* lawyers.
When every firm free-rides on the training pipeline, no one invests in maintaining it.
the verification capacity needed to catch increasingly subtle AI errors is exactly the domain expertise that the collective automation decision is destroying.

kp.k: T-shaped firms could retain a thin human apex
kp.d: A fourth speculative structure emerges if automation advances into work previously treated as judgment: an automated vertical stack topped by a small, horizontally connected human layer orchestrating work and relationships with clients, regulators, consultants and other firms. The authors do not select a winning structure and expect variation by practice, market segment and geography.
qs: The vertical stroke is the automated stack.
The horizontal bar is the human layer --- thin, stretched wide, doing the relational and integrative work that machines can't.
We don't know which shape wins.
We suspect different practice areas and market segments will settle on different structures

kp.k: Integrated expertise requires apprenticeship automation may undermine
kp.d: The essay's central unresolved formation problem is that integrated solutions demand broader expertise across business, strategy, regulation, technology and geopolitics, not merely technical legal competence. The authors argue this requires more apprenticeship and exposure to complex matters, even as automation removes the work through which such experience develops. They leave open whether the profession can reproduce integrative expertise under its proposed new model.
qs: That kind of integrative judgment requires *more* apprenticeship, not less.
The profession's response to automation --- go up, go out, become an integrated solutions provider --- depends on a production process that automation is eliminating.
The automation that makes "up" possible also destroys the pathway to the breadth that "out" requires.
Whether the profession can go up and out while the ladder behind it collapses is the question this piece leaves with the reader.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts and Wilkins argue that automating routine legal production pushes remaining lawyers toward higher-order judgment and multidisciplinary work: 'up and out.'
pts.d: The authors identify contract review, due diligence, first-pass research, drafting and precedent analysis as the technical substrate targeted by AI. Their proposed reorientation combines moving up from production to orchestration with moving out into business, regulatory, financial, reputational and geopolitical dimensions of client problems. This is presented as a developing trajectory, not an established guarantee that the remaining work will sustain the profession.

pts.k: The authors predict that lawyers increasingly become managers and orchestrators of AI rather than primary producers of legal work.
pts.d: Drawing an analogy with software engineering and their earlier experiential essay, Roberts and Wilkins describe lawyers directing, coaching and editing AI output using domain expertise. They frame the orchestrator as distinct from both an augmented worker using a copilot and a replaced worker whose work runs on autopilot: the orchestrator commissions and coordinates both. The extension from software to law is explicitly conditional. They claim AI can make an orchestration role already performed by leading general counsel faster and more scalable.

pts.k: AI is presented as removing some practical barriers to delivering integrated, multidisciplinary solutions, rather than creating the demand for them.
pts.d: Roberts and Wilkins say demand predates generative AI but encountered cultural resistance, restrictions on nonlawyer ownership, difficulties integrating professions physically and constraints on outside investment. Their claimed AI mechanisms are shared digital workspaces, agents handling volume work and technology providing a common platform. They interpret Harvey Shared Spaces as infrastructure for collaboration among law firms, consulting firms and corporate clients and infer that Harvey's ambition extends beyond legal software. They do not establish that AI removes ownership restrictions or that Harvey has already realised this broader strategy.

pts.k: The authors predict new work for in-house lawyers governing autonomous AI agents.
pts.d: As agent adoption expands, corporate legal teams are expected to govern organisational use through liability frameworks, regulatory expectations and risk tolerance. The authors present this as an expanding adjacent domain that can increase law's centrality. Separately, they state that general counsel are already developing their own orchestration capabilities, potentially dispensing with law firms as intermediaries.

pts.k: Moving upmarket exposes law firms to converging competition rather than securing an uncontested refuge.
pts.d: Using Christensen's disruption framework, Roberts and Wilkins argue that technical-work entrants can improve and pursue higher-value work. They identify four sources of competitive pressure: AI-native legal providers, the Big Four's multidisciplinary service businesses, buyer-side general counsel and foundation-model companies' deployment businesses. They suggest AI and big data may activate the Big Four's existing capabilities, while acknowledging that internal ambivalence and strong post-COVID demand for incumbent firms have limited their advance in established markets. Their prediction is competitive convergence, not a settled conclusion that incumbents will lose.

pts.k: The authors describe foundation-model deployment businesses as new competitors delivering integrated services on AI-native economics.
pts.d: The essay reports April–May 2026 developments: a $1.5 billion Anthropic joint venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and Goldman Sachs, and a $4 billion OpenAI deployment company backed by TPG, with consultancy equity participation and staffing through Tomoro's acquisition. Roberts and Wilkins interpret these as forward-deployed engineering businesses embedded in client problems rather than conventional software vendors. They claim such businesses target the cross-domain delivery territory law firms seek, without partnership overhead. These transactions and interpretations are source-reported examples, not independently established findings within the essay.

pts.k: Wilkins's position is that regulatory embedding, institutional trust and professional control slow disruption, while automation may increase demand for high-level legal judgment.
pts.d: The essay attributes to David Wilkins a stronger belief in law's structural defences: licensing, bar rules, opinion-letter requirements, court-access restrictions, partnership governance and trusted relationships. His account predicts slower reconfiguration than in less protected industries. It also offers a conditional complementarity mechanism: more automated contracts and compliance can produce more edge cases, cross-jurisdictional trade-offs and strategic risk decisions requiring human judgment. No quantity of additional demand or net employment effect is estimated.

pts.k: Roberts's contrasting position is that professional protections may delay disruption without preventing AI from moving into judgment work.
pts.d: The essay attributes to Anthea Roberts the view that entrants can route around protections by retaining lawyer oversight while adopting AI-native economics. She points to changes in software-engineering agent capabilities over the preceding eighteen months, Arizona's licensing of KPMG, Utah's regulatory sandbox and the essay's reported May 2026 developments as signs of a moving boundary. The authors explicitly leave unresolved whether legal protections are durable or merely delay a Christensen-style disruption.

pts.k: The authors propose four conditional staffing configurations rather than predicting a single successor to the pyramid.
pts.d: An obelisk retains hierarchy and up-or-out promotion but sharply reduces junior intake. A barbell retains senior relationship-and-judgment lawyers and AI-fluent juniors while squeezing mid-career lawyers, eventually damaging succession. A diamond concentrates experienced orchestrators, reviewers and integrators in the middle, with a smaller junior base and apex. A T arises if automation advances further into judgment: a thin human layer coordinates an automated stack and connects across clients and disciplines. These are scenarios conditional on automation and partial success of 'up and out'; the diamond is a staffing shape, not a competence ideal.

pts.k: Automation risks undermining the apprenticeship and verification expertise on which higher-value AI-enabled legal services depend.
pts.d: Roberts and Wilkins argue that individually rational reductions in junior work can produce collective underinvestment in training: firms want trained lawyers while relying on others to develop them. This threatens both future integrative advisers and the human capacity to check increasingly subtle AI errors. They argue that multidisciplinary judgment needs more apprenticeship, not less, making 'up and out' dependent on a training process automation may eliminate. This is a causal warning and coordination-failure argument rather than a measured finding about training losses.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The essay relies on prior research, illustrative organisational cases, cross-domain experience and conceptual arguments rather than direct quantitative tests of its AI predictions.
pts.d: The authors invoke Wilkins's decade of work on integrated solutions and specifically his 2018 Center on the Legal Profession research on Global 100 firms' marketing. Historical examples include Eversheds's consulting arm, PwC's reported legal presence in 124 countries by 2012 and Bridgewater's reported cost reductions of more than 50 percent through virtual law-firm arrangements; these support pre-existing demand, not measured AI effects. Contemporary illustrations include Harvey Shared Spaces, AI deployment ventures and regulatory openings. Software-engineering experience supplies an analogy for orchestration and an advancing automation frontier. Bek's intelligence/judgment distinction and Christensen's disruption theory supply conceptual frameworks adopted by the authors; quoted third parties are not independent interview subjects here. The essay supplies no legal-AI benchmark results, staffing dataset, quantified productivity study or empirical estimate of the proposed training mechanism.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The essay combines claims of current change in 2026 with undated, conditional forecasts and explicitly unresolved outcomes.
pts.d: The document is dated 2026, its introductory note describes drafting in late March and early April, and its body discusses April–May 2026 developments. Historical demand is traced back at least a decade, with examples from 2012 and 2018. No deadline is offered for wholesale staffing change or displacement. Orchestration depends partly on law following the software pattern; new governance work depends on agent proliferation; complementarity depends on automation generating judgment-intensive problems; the T-shaped structure depends on automation advancing into judgment. The authors expect professional friction to slow legal-market change and variation across practices, market segments and jurisdictions rather than one uniform endpoint.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The analysis centres on elite corporate law firms, their career pipelines, corporate legal buyers and competing integrated-service providers.
pts.d: Junior lawyers face reduced intake and fewer learning-by-doing opportunities, although AI-fluent entrants could retain a role in the barbell scenario. Mid-career lawyers may be squeezed out or become the core of a diamond-shaped orchestration workforce. Partners face both opportunities in judgment-intensive advice and threats to the junior-work economics supporting them. In-house teams gain AI-governance responsibilities and may internalise orchestration formerly supplied by outside firms. Corporate clients may obtain more integrated delivery from AI-native legal providers, Big Four legal businesses or model-company deployment businesses. Harvey is discussed as enabling software infrastructure, distinct from businesses delivering the legal or integrated work. The source does not estimate public access-to-justice benefits or economy-wide employment effects.
